title: Power & Influence 101: office politics playbook from Harvard & Stanford MBAs
summary: Cherie and Jean lay out four workplace power skills nobody teaches at school: listening with empathy, executive presence, building a network of allies and mentors, and negotiation/influence. Each comes with tactics from their time at LinkedIn, Snap and Goldman plus a mini exercise, and they close by addressing the 'ick' of office politics, arguing you must understand the game to play it authentically and to change it once you have power.

ideas.idea: Listening with empathy is the most underrated workplace skill; the trick is not just listening but making the other person feel heard.
ideas.detail: As a cross-functional senior PM at LinkedIn (Jean) and head of product at Snap (Cherie), most of the senior job was managing relationships, which starts with listening; many workplace problems stem from people feeling ignored or overridden.

ideas.idea: Repeat back what someone said ('What I'm hearing is X, did I get that right?') as a forcing function for active listening and to confirm your comprehension.
ideas.detail: It stops you from planning your next point while they talk, lets them correct you, and builds goodwill even when you can't act on their concern. Cherie says it is a good starting method for people who are not naturally empathetic listeners.

ideas.idea: Information is power, and you can't gather information if you're not listening.
ideas.detail: Cherie says she only fully understood this later in her career and returns to it throughout the episode, including in negotiation, where information gathering reveals the other side's real wants.

ideas.idea: Speak last in a meeting, summarize others' points by name, then add your own: it builds consensus and allies because people who are named perk up and back your point.
ideas.detail: Exercise: in a low-stakes meeting say 'what I heard Brittany say was X, Tim said Y, I like that because...' then make your point. Great storytellers are seen as the summarizer who connects everything; referencing others gives them automatic buy-in.

ideas.idea: Executive presence is confidence, calm and gravitas conveyed mostly through nonverbal cues such as eye contact, posture and voice, not what you say.
ideas.detail: The hosts cite studies that people focus more on how you look and sound than on content; it is the number one skill to be taken seriously in any room.

ideas.idea: Where you sit in a meeting tells the room how you perceive your own role; people choose seats strategically, so choose yours deliberately.
ideas.detail: Sit at the table (or next to the top person) to be perceived; sit on the side to stay out of it. Studies show women gravitate to the back; Sheryl Sandberg's 'take a seat at the table'. Jean as a LinkedIn intern note-taker unknowingly took the seat next to CEO Jeff Weiner.

ideas.idea: Meetings are 'kabuki theater': smart people have already coordinated and rehearsed what they will say before the meeting happens.
ideas.detail: Cherie says almost nothing is ad hoc; behind-the-scenes alignment on seating and talking points is normal and not necessarily malicious.

ideas.idea: Reframe nervousness as excitement before a high-stakes presentation; the physical sensations are the same and the label changes the experience.
ideas.detail: Evan Spiegel gave Cherie this tip; Jean learned the same nervous-to-excited reframe in a business school executive presence class and notes studies support it.

ideas.idea: Do a quick burst of cardio (jumping jacks, push-ups, jumping in place) right before presenting to align your racing heart with your body.
ideas.detail: Credited to Jean's former boss Eric Wellenbacher; she no longer power-poses. Public speaking is feared more than death, and matching physical motion to the elevated heart rate makes her feel focused.

ideas.idea: Executive presence is useless without allies in the room, so in any new company deliberately cultivate mentors and allies across every part of the organization, not just your own group.
ideas.detail: Notice who you gravitate toward and who gravitates toward you, then lean in; a network spread across the company is far more powerful than one concentrated in your team.

ideas.idea: Never open with 'will you be my mentor?'; let mentorship emerge organically after two or three coffee chats where you bring real questions.
ideas.detail: A direct ask is jarring when the person doesn't know you. The exception is a formal mentor-matching program, which is like an explicitly romantic date. Jean keeps a tracker of admired colleagues to reach out to and follows up if they don't reply.

ideas.idea: Ask your friends who their mentors are and get introduced, and seek mentors in other orgs who can sponsor you from a different vantage point.
ideas.detail: Early at Goldman in investment management, Cherie asked a friend in sales and trading about her mentor Teresa, got an intro, and built a lasting relationship; senior people are often eager to mentor juniors because any skill can help them.

ideas.idea: Come to every mentor conversation with an explicit agenda of two or three things you want, which earns you the mentor's network and resources.
ideas.detail: A mentee who asked Jean what she was watching on Netflix left her feeling unhelpful; a prepared, directive mentee signals they won't waste the time of anyone the mentor introduces them to, so mentors open up their network.

ideas.idea: Negotiation and influence is the 'final boss' skill that only works once you have listened, built a network and developed presence; it starts with knowing your own resources and everyone else's.
ideas.detail: At Snap, Cherie and colleague Jeff were pulled into a last-minute exec presentation in New York; she worried about building slides until she learned Jeff had a team that excelled at decks, so they split content and production.

ideas.idea: Most negotiations are not zero-sum: gather information on what the other side actually wants and you can both get 100% (the orange peel and the juice) instead of splitting 50/50.
ideas.detail: From Jean's Stanford negotiation class with Michele Gelfand: splitting an orange in half satisfies no one, but if Sally wants the peel for dessert and you want the juice, both win fully. Applies to comp talks too, where a manager may have more room on bonus than salary.

ideas.idea: Three-step influence framework: research the other party's goals and KPIs, frame your ask so it helps them hit those goals, then enter ready to trade off and invent creative solutions.
ideas.detail: The hosts note 'negotiation' sounds adversarial but every conversation is really a negotiation; in a comp talk, start from the shared premise that both sides want you to stay and grow at the company.

ideas.idea: These tactics are the unsaid rules of the modern corporate workplace; if you didn't learn them from family, you must learn them yourself and at least recognize when they're used on you.
ideas.detail: The sisters had no parent or family insider to teach them the professional world's inner workings and sought mentors instead. Start with one skill rather than all four at once; the tactics apply to any sector, not just finance and tech.

ideas.idea: Office politics feels 'icky', but you can only change a system once you hold power in it, which requires understanding the landscape first.
ideas.detail: Cherie cites Stanford GSB professor Jeffrey Pfeffer's book on power: play within the rules of the existing framework to reach a position from which you can change it.

ideas.idea: The ick disappears when you truly believe in your mission, and you should stay within your own values rather than going Machiavellian.
ideas.detail: Jean uses tactics only in service of what she believes is best for the business or team; Cherie has seen leaders take politics too far and lost respect for them, while others do it authentically and earn more respect.
